title: Pocket Sound Amplifiers for Restaurants, Church and One-on-One Talks
subtitle: A small handheld amplifier can make a nearby voice easier to hear, as long as you know what it is and what it is not.
excerpt: A pocket sound amplifier is a simple box with a microphone and headphones that makes nearby sound louder. Here is how it works, how it differs from a hearing aid, and what the two listings we found cost.
author: Nickel And Gadget Editors

sections.content: Picture leaning in across a restaurant table, asking someone to repeat themselves a third time, and still missing half of what was said. Or imagine a speaker's voice fading at the end of each sentence, so you spend the service guessing. Moments like these can be tiring.

One simple tool for these situations is a personal sound amplifier, often shortened to PSAP. It is a small box you hold or set down, with a microphone that picks up nearby sound and headphones that deliver it louder to your ears. No phone or app is needed.

One caution up front: the FDA says these devices are intended for people with normal hearing. If you notice hearing loss, see your doctor or an audiologist (a hearing specialist) before you buy anything.

The idea is plain. A microphone on the device listens, a small amplifier makes the sound louder, and you hear it through headphones or earphones plugged into the box. You turn the controls to set the volume.

The Pocketalker 2.0 models in this guide also have a T-coil, a tiny built-in receiver that works with hearing loops. A hearing loop is a wire system that some churches, theaters and meeting rooms install to send sound to listeners' devices. Ask the venue whether it has one.

There is one big limit. An amplifier raises everything near its microphone, including clattering dishes and the next table's laughter. It tends to help most face to face or in a quiet small group, and much less in a crowded, noisy room.
Pocket amplifier or OTC hearing aid?

These are different things. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) treats sound amplifiers as consumer electronics, not medical devices, so quality can vary more than with hearing aids. It also says they are not alternatives to hearing aids. The FDA's consumer page includes a table comparing prescription and over-the-counter (OTC) hearing aids with amplifiers. We cover OTC hearing aids in a separate guide.

"PSAPs, in contrast, are intended for people with normal hearing to amplify sounds in certain situations." — FDA consumer update, "Hearing Aids and Personal Sound Amplification Products: What to Know"

If you suspect your hearing has changed, Consumer Reports recommends a professional hearing test first, and an audiologist can help you choose. In 2017, the magazine tested five PSAPs against a prescription hearing aid. It reported that "Not all of the tested PSAPs aided hearing." That test is old, so treat it as background, not a verdict on today's products.

items: Check what is in the box. The no-accessories version comes without headphones or earphones, which add $30 to $37.
Look at the controls. The maker describes the Pocketalker 2.0's controls as large and manageable.

Ask about batteries. It runs on two AAA batteries, and the maker lists up to 105 hours with alkaline. Two spare AAA batteries (BAT 010-2) are $10.00 from the maker. A rechargeable kit is extra, and we do not have its price.
See whether it has a T-coil if you attend a place with a hearing loop.
Note the maximum gain, the most it can boost sound, measured in decibels (dB). It is 63 dB on this model, so start with the volume low.
Read the return policy and warranty before buying, and compare prices, since listings for the same model vary.

sections.content: A note on range: this guide covers two listings of one model, the Pocketalker 2.0, at $265.00 and $250.00. Other listings we saw ran from $245 to $279, so check current price before you buy. We do not have a lower-cost option to offer here.
Setting it up and using it well

Put the batteries in, plug in the headphones, and turn the volume all the way down before putting them on. Then raise it slowly while someone talks to you. Starting low matters because a strong amplifier can make sharp sounds, like a dropped fork, uncomfortably loud.

Try it first in a quiet room with one person, so you get used to the volume before using it out and about. The maker also sells a 12-foot microphone extension (WCA 007, $22.00) if you want to place the microphone away from the device.
Keep in mind that this is not a Bluetooth phone accessory, and it does have cords. If your main goal is phone calls or a cord-free fit, a different kind of device is likely a better match.
The Pocketalker 2.0 is rated to work between 41°F and 104°F, so do not leave it in a hot or freezing car. Keep spare AAA batteries in your bag.
sections.label: Good to Know

sections.content: A pocket amplifier does not treat hearing loss, but it may make a one-on-one conversation a little less work. If voices seem muffled more often than not, a hearing test is a sensible next step.
